Training in the Venkatesh Lab has been an incredibly rewarding and transformative experience for me, both scientifically and personally. The lab provided an environment that encouraged curiosity, independence, and critical thinking. I had the opportunity to work on several projects simultaneously, both collaborative and independent, which helped me develop strong scientific rigor, adaptability, and project management skills.
During my tenure, I gained extensive technical expertise alongside the interpersonal and professional skills required in academia. One of the most unique aspects of the lab is its non-hierarchical structure, which allows everyone to freely exchange ideas, discuss science openly, and create an atmosphere where one constantly learns from others while also contributing back to the group. This culture fosters confidence, creativity, and intellectual growth.

The lab environment is highly motivating and collaborative, with driven scientists who are passionate about their work. The pace of research is fast and dynamic, which continuously pushes one to think efficiently, troubleshoot independently, and work effectively as part of a team. At the same time, the environment remains supportive rather than competitive in a toxic way, making it a genuinely enjoyable place to learn and conduct research.
Beyond technical training, the lab significantly shaped my growth as a researcher and communicator. Everyone is encouraged to share data regularly in weekly lab meetings, critically analyze literature, discuss experiments, mentor juniors/trainees, and actively participate in discussions and journal clubs. These experiences greatly improved my confidence, scientific communication, and ability to approach research questions thoughtfully and independently.

Overall, my experience in the Venkatesh Lab has had a profound impact on my development as a scientist. The mentorship, collaborative spirit, and exposure to interdisciplinary research have provided me with a strong foundation for pursuing a future career in regenerative biology and neuroscience research.

Before applying, the first and most important step was understanding the field of spinal cord injury and identifying where my interests fit within it. As a mentor, Ishwariya Ma’am made sure that everyone in the lab was aware of researchers and laboratories actively working in different parts of the world.

From my personal experience, before sending each application email, I always discussed it with Ishwariya Ma’am and asked for her feedback. Her suggestions were extremely helpful because she understood my strengths as a candidate and could guide me on whether a particular position or program would be a good fit for me. She also ensured that each application was submitted within the stipulated deadline. I was also able to use the lab space for interview appearances, which was a great support.

After interviews, my discussions with her always helped me focus on the positive aspects and improve further. Most importantly, she never discouraged me, even when I received rejections from different positions. That constant encouragement was extremely important during the application process.

Receiving admission was very important to me because it represented not only an academic opportunity, but also a step forward in my scientific career and personal growth. Throughout the process, Ishwariya Ma’am remained a constant source of support until I was finally placed. Even today, I feel comfortable asking her for advice on both scientific and non-scientific matters. She was my mentor, she is my mentor, and she will always remain my mentor.
column18:
My training in the Venkatesh Lab has been an extremely enriching and meaningful experience. As a candidate, the lab does not expect prior training in neuroscience or spinal cord injury. Anyone with a basic understanding of biology and a willingness to learn can grow and excel during their training in the Venkatesh Lab.

One of the most special aspects of the lab is the way the entire group works together. The environment always feels like a family. The lab has exceptional PhD students, postdoctoral fellows, research assistants, and project assistants, each with specific responsibilities. Everyone is supportive and always willing to guide you, check on your progress, and help ensure that you are learning and performing experiments correctly.

As a trainee, both the lab and the overall environment at CSIR-CCMB provide the freedom to perform, think independently, and develop decision-making skills. Most importantly, Ishwariya Ma’am ensures that every candidate gets the opportunity to grow, build confidence, and create their own scientific identity. Her support has been constant, and words are not enough to describe the impact she has had as a mentor.

Beyond research, the lab also believes in creating memories and celebrating each other’s small and big achievements, whether it is a grant celebration, birthday celebration, or lab retreat. Anyone who has been part of this lab would agree that every member is valued and respected. The Venkatesh Lab is more than just a workplace; it is a family that eats together, learns together, and grows together.
column20:
Yes, I firmly believe that the monetary investment towards the PBST/dissertation fee was worth it for me.

During 2023–24, I paid a total of ₹80,000 for my dissertation training. In return, I had the opportunity to stay for 12 months in CCMB accommodation and use the transportation facilities completely free of cost. I believe that when a place provides the right environment for learning, growth, and professional development, the investment becomes truly worthwhile.

At CCMB, I had access to exceptional microscopy facilities and received valuable training in several important areas, including animal handling and cell culture. All of these experiences were included within the same amount. Therefore, when I compare the fee with the exposure, training, and lessons I received, I feel that ₹80,000 was much less than the actual value of the experience.

Speaking specifically about the Venkatesh Lab, I have no regrets at all. I honestly do not think I could have received a better training opportunity. The experience, mentorship, scientific exposure, and personal growth I gained cannot be measured only in terms of money. In fact, if I compare the investment with what I received in return, I feel I gained much more than what I paid for.

column18:
I joined the Venkatesh Lab not fully knowing what I was walking into. What followed was one of the most transformative periods of my life,  scientifically, intellectually, and personally.
It started with cloning experiments on just four genes. Dr Ishwariya (Ma'am) worked right alongside us, demonstrating key steps with patience and enthusiasm. When all four targets were successfully cloned, I felt a pride I hadn't quite experienced before. Since then, I've lost count of how many cloning experiments I've done, but every small win still feels worth celebrating. Guess who taught me that? Ma'am.
From molecular biology, I moved into tissue culture, learning HEK293 and Neuro2a cell culture, as well as transfections and transductions. Then came one of our bigger challenges: AAV production. Commercial AAVs cost ₹1 lakh per construct, and with multiple constructs needed, that wasn't feasible. So Ma'am, Sanjana, and I got trained together on in-house production. Our early titers were frustratingly low. But we kept troubleshooting, and on one Valentine's Day, I finally hit a titer of 10⁹. We had brought AAV production in-house at one-third the commercial cost. That day stays with me.
Along the way, I also learned tissue processing, vibratome and cryosectioning of brain and spinal cord tissue, confocal and bright-field microscopy, and image analysis using ImageJ and Zeiss software. I overcame my initial hesitation about animal work and learned stereotaxic surgery, a delicate technique for delivering viral vectors into precise brain regions.
One of our proudest team moments was performing single-cell ATAC-Seq, a first at CCMB. We planned every detail meticulously, and on the day, everything came together perfectly. It was one of those rare moments in science where the hard work and the timing align, and you get to share it with people you genuinely care about.
I also explored single-cell bioinformatics, not an easy space to enter, and picked up science communication skills along the way: designing research posters, writing abstracts, presenting at lab meetings and open days, and learning to use BioRender and AI tools for scientific visualisation. On the organisational side, I managed reagent inventory, coordinated vendor procurement, and applied project planning tools like Gantt charts and the Eisenhower Matrix to keep experiments on track.
But the result that none of us will forget came from our regeneration experiments. When Yogesh's slides showed green axons visibly crossing the spinal cord injury site, the entire lab was in awe. That wasn't just data. That was the moment we knew regeneration was possible, and that everything we had worked toward meant something real.
What made all of this possible was the environment Dr Ishwariya created. When experiments failed, and they often did, she never showed frustration. She would say, "It's okay. We'll troubleshoot." She celebrated with us, guided us through the hard parts, and gave us space to grow into ourselves as scientists. She treated each of us like her own.
For anyone considering an internship, project, or PhD: find the right mentor. The experiments matter. The results matter. But the person who shapes how you think, how you handle failure, and how you show up every day? That changes everything. I was lucky. I found mine.
column20: Honestly, yes, without hesitation. When I first considered the fee, I did pause and weigh it carefully. But looking back, what I received in return wasn't just lab access or a certificate. I was trained across an extraordinary breadth of techniques and skills that would have taken years to piece together elsewhere, if at all. More than the techniques, I learned how to think through a problem, how to stay steady when experiments fail, and how to be part of a real, functioning research team working on meaningful science. I watched axons regenerate. I contributed to work that had never been done at CCMB before. I left with a CV, a poster, publications-in-progress, and a mentor I will carry with me for the rest of my career. The fee bought me a seat at a table where real science happens, and that is genuinely priceless.
column21:
I just want to say, I came in as someone who had studied biology in theory but had never really done science. I leave knowing how to troubleshoot a failed experiment at 11 pm without panicking, how to plan a full experimental timeline, and how to sit with uncertainty and keep going anyway. That shift didn't happen because of any single protocol I learned. It happened because of the environment Ma'am created.
Also, the non-science stuff matters more than I expected. Learning how to make a poster, write an abstract, manage lab inventory, plan with Gantt charts, and present at Open Day, these felt like "extras" at the time. They're not. They're what make you functional in a real research setting, and I'm grateful they were built into the programme.
And honestly, if you're reading this, Ma'am, thank you for never making me feel bad for not knowing something, and for always making the lab feel like a place worth showing up to.

My time at the Venkatesh Lab was unforgettable, truly the best experience I could have hoped for. I went in expecting to complete a project and move on, but I found myself deeply engaged with work that genuinely excited me. The combination of wet lab and dry lab work gave me comprehensive exposure to both hands-on and computational research.
The pace of the lab was fast-moving, which meant I accomplished far more than I anticipated in a single year. I attended two conferences, presenting a poster at a mini symposium, which was my first major presentation experience. Throughout this journey, I received complete support for my presentations and thesis defense, which helped me develop critical soft skills, learning how to visualize complex ideas and communicate them effectively to both scientific and non-scientific audiences.
Beyond the fascinating field itself, the techniques I worked on were truly cutting-edge. I gained hands-on training in animal handling, genomics techniques, data analysis, and so much more. I honestly don't think any other lab would offer such comprehensive technical training.
What made the experience truly special was the people. The lab became my second family. I formed friendships with people now scattered across the world, but we remain connected and ready to support each other. Additionally, I received incredible support for my Master's applications, from reference letters to interview preparation to feedback on my motivation letter. The collaborative spirit here is what made all the difference.
